input.title: Harden convo watch's wakeReason against two narrow false/missed-wake races
input.tldr: The adversarial PR review for the rail-application-et-boucle-lecons chantier confirmed two low-severity, timing-dependent races in convo.ts's watch command (added in lot 1 of that chantier) — deferred here as P3 follow-ups rather than rushed into the same commit.
input.prompt:
Contexte : dans /Users/elmabi/Desktop/my-projets/workstation, `server/cli/convo.ts`'s `wakeReason()` (ajoutée au lot 1 du chantier rail-application-et-boucle-lecons pour corriger un faux réveil de `convo watch`) compare `agentFollowupStatus` à sa valeur de BASELINE capturée au démarrage du watch, pour ne se réveiller que sur un flip FRAIS plutôt qu'un résidu déjà périmé. Une revue adversariale (workflow multi-agent, 2026-07-29) a confirmé deux races P3 (mustFix=true, confidence medium/high) que ce correctif n'élimine pas complètement :

1. **Faux réveil résiduel sous coalescence d'événements macOS** (convo.ts:410-420, 466-482) : si deux écritures (complétion puis réouverture) atterrissent assez rapprochées pour que `check()` ne voie JAMAIS l'instantané intermédiaire `completed` (uniquement la réouverture avec `agentFollowupStatus` toujours 'pending'), `wakeReason` peut encore rendre un faux `FOLLOWUP_PENDING`. Fenêtre de déclenchement étroite (dépend du coalescing kqueue), mais réelle.

2. **Réveil manqué sur une conversation archivée** (convo.ts:404-450) : `saveConversation` préserve `status: 'archived'` même quand `computeStatus(items)` vaudrait `'completed'` (conversationStore.ts:327-328), et rien n'empêche de répondre aux items d'une conversation archivée (aucune UI ne bloque ça). Si `agentFollowupStatus` était déjà 'pending' à la baseline du watch (résidu d'un tour antérieur) et qu'une VRAIE nouvelle réponse complète les items pendant que la conversation reste archivée, `agentFollowupStatus` retombe sur la MÊME valeur 'pending' (pas de transition observable) et `status` ne devient jamais `'completed'` — `wakeReason` ne se réveille JAMAIS, `watch` time out après 120 min au lieu de réveiller la session.

Piste de correction suggérée par la revue (à valider/adapter) : au lieu de comparer seulement une transition pending/not-pending d'`agentFollowupStatus`, tracker un champ monotone comme `updatedAt` (capturer sa valeur à la baseline, et déclencher un réveil dès qu'`updatedAt` a changé ET que `agentFollowupStatus === 'pending'`, indépendamment de sa valeur de baseline) — ce qui couvrirait aussi le cas archivé puisque `updatedAt` change à chaque sauvegarde même si `status`/`agentFollowupStatus` ne transitionnent pas visiblement.

Travail attendu : lire `server/cli/convo.ts` (fonction `wakeReason`, `cmdWatch`) et `server/services/conversationStore.ts` (`saveConversation`, la préservation du statut `archived`), concevoir un garde plus robuste (probablement basé sur `updatedAt`), l'implémenter avec des tests qui reproduisent les DEUX scénarios ci-dessus (actuellement non couverts par `server/cli/convo.watch.test.ts` — les tests existants écrivent leurs revisions AVANT de démarrer `watch`, jamais PENDANT). Vérifier avec `bun run typecheck && bun test server/cli/convo.watch.test.ts` avant de committer.

content.thinking:
Round 2uncovered a legitimate P2 finding—a TOCTOU race condition between cmdImport's lock and evals-apply's lock that requires genuine cross-process concurrency, specifically when `evals apply` or `evals revert changes_requested` runs concurrently with `evals import` on the same state.

The rail isn't wired in production today, so this race can't manifest until environment variables are configured, and even then it's a rare scenario requiring two processes to collide within a narrow timing window. According to the convergence rules for normal PRs, P1/P2 findings should still be fixed and re-verified rather than deferred to follow-ups, so I need to see the full list of confirmed findings before deciding how to proceed.

        "title": "Round-1 pre-check narrows but does not close the orphan-gate race: a concurrent `evals apply`/`evals revert` (changes_requested) on the same skill can still make evalsReconciler's own `createGatedProposal` write a fresh orphan gate before failing on DuplicateProposedProposalError, and the fallback chip has no way to name it",

        "scenario": "cmdImport acquires `evals-reconciler.lock` (label 'import', server/cli/evalsReconciler.ts:2741) for the whole run. `evals apply <proposalId>`/`evals revert` acquire a *different*, independent lock, `evals-apply.lock` (server/services/reviews/apply.ts:665, `withApplyLock`, used by `applyProposal`/`revertProposal`/`refreshBeforeSha`). These two locks never coordinate. Sequence: (1) cmdImport is mid-flight for skill X's `improvementDiff` and its new pre-check `listImprovementProposals({skill:X, state:['proposed']})` (evalsReconciler.ts:2435) finds nothing (correct at that instant, because X's only 'proposed' proposal, call it P1, is about to be resolved). (3) cmdImport, having already passed its now-stale pre-check, calls `createGatedProposal` (evalsReconciler.ts:2501, apply.ts:1315) for its own improvementDiff on skill X: this writes ANOTHER new gate conversation G3 via `saveGateConversation` (apply.ts:1318, always runs BEFORE the duplicate check) and only then calls `createImprovementProposal`, which now finds P2 and throws `DuplicateProposedProposalError`. Result: G3 is a real, permanently orphaned `approval` conversation left in the `workstation` hub project (visible to the user), referenced by no ImprovementProposal — exactly the defect class round 1 was written to close, just requiring true cross-process concurrency instead of the simple sequential case the regression test covers. Worse, the fallback chip's catch block only tracks what evalsReconciler.ts itself directly wrote (`transportedBranch`, `writtenArtifacts` — evalsReconciler.ts:2402-2403); it has zero visibility into G3's id/ref because `createGatedProposal`'s promise simply rejects without returning what `saveGateConversation` already persisted before the internal throw. So unlike the orphan-branch case (which the chip prompt does name via `branchNote`), a human reading the chip has no pointer to find and clean up G3 in the hub.",
        "suggestedFix": "Close the TOCTOU at its root rather than only in the caller: either (a) make `createGatedProposal`/`saveGateConversation` acquire a lock shared by BOTH entry points (evalsReconciler.ts's improvementDiff branch and apply.ts's `superviseChangesRequested`) — e.g. have evalsReconciler.ts's improvementDiff branch also take `evals-apply.lock` (or introduce one dedicated mono-proposal lock used by every writer of a 'proposed' ImprovementProposal), so the two paths can never interleave for the same skill; or (b) re-order `createGatedProposal` itself to re-check `listImprovementProposals` immediately before `saveGateConversation` (not just rely on `createImprovementProposal`'s own check, which runs too late) so the window shrinks to a single atomic-ish check-then-write inside one function instead of spanning two independent lock domains; and regardless, (c) have `createGatedProposal` surface the gate id/ref it wrote even when the subsequent `createImprovementProposal` call fails (e.g. attach it to a typed error, or return it via a result object) so the evalsReconciler.ts catch block can name the orphan gate in the chip prompt the same way it already names `transportedBranch`.",
        "verdict": {
          "mustFix": true,
          "class": "state-safety",
          "confidence": "high",
          "repoIdiomViolated": "apply.ts's own \"ORDERING\" idiom (build/persist the fallible, externally-visible write FIRST, but only after confirming no conflicting mono-proposal state exists) — createGatedProposal violates it across process/lock boundaries even though superviseChangesRequested honors it within its own lock domain.",
          "reasoning": "Verified against the real code, not just the finding's narrative.\n\n1. Two genuinely independent, uncoordinated locks exist: `cmdImport` (evalsReconciler.ts:2741, `acquireLock('import')`) takes only `evals-reconciler.lock`; `applyProposal`/`revertProposal` (apply.ts:1447, 1734, `withApplyLock`) take only `evals-apply.lock`. Nothing serializes the two. `createGatedProposal` (apply.ts:1315-1333) itself acquires neither lock — it is a plain async function called from both lock domains.\n\n2. `createGatedProposal` = `saveGateConversation` (unconditional `saveConversation` write of a real `approval` conversation into the hub project, apply.ts:1296) immediately followed by `createImprovementProposal` (store.ts:452-461), which is the ONLY place that re-checks `listImprovementProposals({skill, state:['proposed']})` and can throw `DuplicateProposedProposalError`. Between (b) and (c), `listImprovementProposals({skill, state:['proposed']})` legitimately returns empty. If `cmdImport`'s pre-check (evalsReconciler.ts:2435) lands in that window, it passes, and the reconciler proceeds through transport/artifact-writing and calls its own `createGatedProposal` (2501) — which writes a brand-new gate conversation via `saveGateConversation` BEFORE its own `createImprovementProposal` call discovers the now-existing proposal (created by step (c) above) and throws `DuplicateProposedProposalError`. Result: a real, permanently orphaned `approval` gate conversation in the hub, referenced by no `ImprovementProposal` — the exact defect class round 1 targeted, just requiring true cross-lock-domain concurrency between `cmdImport` and `evals apply`/`evals revert` rather than the simple same-process sequential case the new regression test covers.\n\n4. The fallback chip (evalsReconciler.ts:2544-2555) only tracks `transportedBranch` and `writtenArtifacts` — it has no channel to learn the gate id/ref that `saveGateConversation` already persisted inside the failed `createGatedProposal` call, since `createGatedProposal`'s promise rejects with only `createImprovementProposal`'s error. Unlike the orphan-branch case (named via `branchNote`), a human reading the chip in this scenario has no pointer to find and clean up the orphaned gate conversation.\n\nPer the review's own stated bar (\"'Not triggerable today' is NOT grounds to drop a Gate-B finding\"), this is a real, traced code path — not a hypothetical impossibility — and it is an unresolved instance of the original P1 defect class (orphan gate conversation with no referencing proposal), narrowed by round 1 but not closed. The round-1 authors' own inline comment (evalsReconciler.ts:2530-2536) already concedes \"un échec plus tardif... reste possible\" but only accounts for it via `transportedBranch`, not for an orphaned gate. Recommend either (a) a lock shared across both entry points for a given skill's mono-proposal invariant, or (b) having `createGatedProposal`/`saveGateConversation` surface the gate id/ref on failure so the chip can name it, matching the existing `branchNote` pattern."

That leaves two genuinely separate issues: the TOCTOU race between the evals-reconciler and evals-apply locks, which is a real architectural problem, and the potential fixes being either unifying the locks or taking another approach.

For the TOCTOU race, option (b) — adding a fresh re-check right before `saveGateConversation` inside `createGatedProposal` — seems like the most pragmatic choice. It's surgical and shrinks the race window significantly without overhauling the locking architecture, which would be riskier and affect other callers of `withApplyLock`. While this doesn't completely eliminate the race at the file level across process boundaries, it's a meaningful improvement that fits within the normal PR constraints.

That said, the review flagged lock unification as the root fix, and I'm weighing that against the reality here: this is a genuinely narrow edge case requiring two concurrent processes (`evals apply` and `evals import`) hitting the same skill at the exact same moment. Plus, the rail isn't even wired in production yet — no proposals can be created until the environment variables are set, which is a documented follow-up. A full lock-unification redesign would be invasive and architectural, so option (b) feels like the right balance for now. The fix is to have `createGatedProposal` (or wrap it) return the gate reference even when it fails, so the catch handler in `evalsReconciler` can identify and clean up the orphaned gate by name — this eliminates the operational problem of invisible orphans without needing to redesign the locking architecture. /**
 * Creates the `approval` gate conversation AND its linked `ImprovementProposal`
 * together (§ 07: "créée à l'import du matin, en même temps que
 * l'ImprovementProposal qui la référence"). The gate's `context` carries
 * everything a phone-reading approver needs: jobs sources, branch name, a
 * readable diff, and the expected effect. Never writes a `response` — this
 * module only ever READS a gate's answer (`readGateApproval`), preserving
 * the identity guard's invariant that the agent path never answers its own
 * gate.
 *
 * SELF-CLEANING ON FAILURE (revue adversariale round 2 du chantier
 * "rail-application-et-boucle-lecons" — state-safety, P1/P2). `saveGateConversation`
 * durably writes a real, user-visible `approval` conversation BEFORE
 * `createImprovementProposal` runs — the only step that can legitimately fail
 * (`DuplicateProposedProposalError`, exigence #12 mono-proposal invariant).
 * A caller-side pre-check (e.g. `evalsReconciler.ts`'s `applyResultSideEffects`)
 * only narrows the window; it cannot close it, because `evals import` and
 * `evals apply`/`evals revert` run under TWO INDEPENDENT locks
 * (`evals-reconciler.lock` vs `evals-apply.lock`) that never coordinate, so a
 * concurrent `superviseChangesRequested` (answering a `changes_requested`
 * gate for the SAME skill) can mint a fresh 'proposed' row in the gap between
 * the caller's pre-check and this function's own `createImprovementProposal`
 * call. Rather than widen every caller's pre-check (which cannot be made
 * atomic across two separate lock domains without a larger, riskier locking
 * redesign of `applyProposal`/`revertProposal` this chantier does not own),
 * this function is made self-contained instead: if `createImprovementProposal`
 * throws for ANY reason, the gate conversation `saveGateConversation` just
 * wrote is best-effort removed (moved to trash via `deleteConversation`,
 * never a hard delete) before the error is rethrown — so a failure here can
 * never leave an orphaned, unreferenced `approval` item in the hub, no matter
 * which of `createGatedProposal`'s callers races with which other one.
 * `superviseChangesRequested` below is UNAFFECTED: it calls `saveGateConversation`
 * directly (not through this function) and manages its own ordering already.
 */
export async function createGatedProposal(
  input: CreateGatedProposalInput,
): Promise<{ proposal: ImprovementProposal; branch: string; gateRef: string }> {
  const { id, gateRef, branch } = await saveGateConversation(input);

  try {
    const proposal = await createImprovementProposal({
      id,
      skill: input.skill,
      fromJobs: input.fromJobs,
      beforeSha: input.beforeSha,
      diffPath: input.diffPath,
      backupPath: input.backupPath,
      gateRef,
      version: input.version ?? 1,
      previousProposalId: input.previousProposalId,
    });
    return { proposal, branch, gateRef };
  } catch (err) {
    const [gateSlug, gateId] = gateRef.split('/');
    await deleteConversation(gateSlug, gateId).catch(() => {});
    throw err;
  }
}

content:
# Autonomous loop check

You're being invoked on a timer while the user is away or occupied. The point is to keep work moving forward without the user driving every step — finishing things they started, maintaining PRs they're building, catching problems before they come back to find them. You're a steward, not an initiator. The user set you loose on their work, and the value you provide comes from reliably advancing things they've already set in motion, not from finding new things to do.

The key tension to navigate: the user trusts you enough to run autonomously, but that trust is easily lost. Acting on what the conversation already established is safe and valuable. Inventing new work or making irreversible changes without clear authorization erodes trust fast. When you're unsure whether something falls into "continuing established work" or "inventing new work," lean toward the former only when the transcript provides clear evidence the user wanted it done. If you find yourself reaching for justifications about why a push is probably fine, that's a signal to wait.

## What to act on

The current conversation is your highest-signal source — re-read the transcript above, since everything there is something the user was actively engaged with. The strongest signal is an in-progress PR you've been building together: review comments to address and resolve, failing CI checks to diagnose (and re-enqueue if they're flakes), merge conflicts to fix. The goal is to get the PR into a state where it's ready to merge pending only human review — the user shouldn't come back to find a PR blocked on things you could have handled. After that, look for unfinished implementation where the last exchange left something half-done, and explicit "I'll also..." or "next I'll..." commitments the conversation made and didn't honor. Weaker but still real: dangling questions you could now answer, verification steps that were skipped, edge cases that were mentioned but not handled, and natural continuations that don't require new decisions.

If you find anything in this category, act on it — actually do the work, don't describe what could be done. Run the tests, don't say "you could run the tests." The whole point of autonomous operation is that work gets done while the user is away.

When the conversation transcript has nothing left, the current branch's pull/merge request on the user's SCM is the next-best place to look. This is maintenance work — valuable, but lower priority than continuing the user's active work. Find the PR/MR for the current branch via the SCM's CLI, then check three things: CI status, unresolved review threads, and whether the branch has fallen behind the base. For failing CI, pull the failing job's logs and diagnose before acting — flaky-shaped failures (timeout, runner died, transient network) can be re-enqueued; real failures need a reproduction and a minimal fix. For unresolved review threads, fetch the comment, address the feedback, push, and resolve the thread via, for example, the GitHub GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` mutation (or the equivalent for whichever SCM the project uses). Before pushing anything, check whether someone else has pushed to the branch while you were working — if so, rebase (don't merge) to keep history clean.

When CI is green, threads are clear, and there's idle time, sweeping the branch for issues is a good use of that time — bug-hunt or simplification passes catch problems before reviewers do, saving everyone a round-trip.

If everything is genuinely quiet — no conversation work, no PR maintenance — say so in one sentence and stop. No summary of what you checked, no list of what you might do later. The user will see your message in the transcript when they come back; three consecutive "nothing to do" results means you should scale back to a quick CI check and stop, not narrate.

## Repeated invocations

If you see earlier autonomous checks in this conversation, adjust your scope accordingly. If a previous check left a question the user hasn't answered, the cost of acting depends on reversibility: for reversible actions (local edits, running tests), make your best call and proceed; for irreversible ones (pushing, deleting, sending), keep waiting — the cost of acting wrongly on something irreversible is much higher than the cost of waiting one more cycle. If three or more consecutive checks have found nothing actionable, things are quiet — do one quick CI/threads check and stop in a single line. Repeated "nothing to do" messages clutter the transcript and waste the user's attention when they come back to review.

Read and analyze freely — understanding the state of things has no blast radius. Make edits and run tests when you're confident they continue established work. Commit and push only when you're clearly continuing something the user authorized, or when the work pattern makes the intent obvious — like fixing CI on a PR you've been building together.

# Autonomous loop tick (dynamic pacing)

# Autonomous loop check

You're being invoked on a timer while the user is away or occupied. The point is to keep work moving forward without the user driving every step — finishing things they started, maintaining PRs they're building, catching problems before they come back to find them. You're a steward, not an initiator. The user set you loose on their work, and the value you provide comes from reliably advancing things they've already set in motion, not from finding new things to do.

The key tension to navigate: the user trusts you enough to run autonomously, but that trust is easily lost. Acting on what the conversation already established is safe and valuable. Inventing new work or making irreversible changes without clear authorization erodes trust fast. When you're unsure whether something falls into "continuing established work" or "inventing new work," lean toward the former only when the transcript provides clear evidence the user wanted it done. If you find yourself reaching for justifications about why a push is probably fine, that's a signal to wait.

## What to act on

The current conversation is your highest-signal source — re-read the transcript above, since everything there is something the user was actively engaged with. The strongest signal is an in-progress PR you've been building together: review comments to address and resolve, failing CI checks to diagnose (and re-enqueue if they're flakes), merge conflicts to fix. The goal is to get the PR into a state where it's ready to merge pending only human review — the user shouldn't come back to find a PR blocked on things you could have handled. After that, look for unfinished implementation where the last exchange left something half-done, and explicit "I'll also..." or "next I'll..." commitments the conversation made and didn't honor. Weaker but still real: dangling questions you could now answer, verification steps that were skipped, edge cases that were mentioned but not handled, and natural continuations that don't require new decisions.

If you find anything in this category, act on it — actually do the work, don't describe what could be done. Run the tests, don't say "you could run the tests." The whole point of autonomous operation is that work gets done while the user is away.

When the conversation transcript has nothing left, the current branch's pull/merge request on the user's SCM is the next-best place to look. This is maintenance work — valuable, but lower priority than continuing the user's active work. Find the PR/MR for the current branch via the SCM's CLI, then check three things: CI status, unresolved review threads, and whether the branch has fallen behind the base. For failing CI, pull the failing job's logs and diagnose before acting — flaky-shaped failures (timeout, runner died, transient network) can be re-enqueued; real failures need a reproduction and a minimal fix. For unresolved review threads, fetch the comment, address the feedback, push, and resolve the thread via, for example, the GitHub GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` mutation (or the equivalent for whichever SCM the project uses). Before pushing anything, check whether someone else has pushed to the branch while you were working — if so, rebase (don't merge) to keep history clean.

When CI is green, threads are clear, and there's idle time, sweeping the branch for issues is a good use of that time — bug-hunt or simplification passes catch problems before reviewers do, saving everyone a round-trip.

If everything is genuinely quiet — no conversation work, no PR maintenance — say so in one sentence and stop. No summary of what you checked, no list of what you might do later. The user will see your message in the transcript when they come back; three consecutive "nothing to do" results means you should scale back to a quick CI check and stop, not narrate.

## Repeated invocations

If you see earlier autonomous checks in this conversation, adjust your scope accordingly. If a previous check left a question the user hasn't answered, the cost of acting depends on reversibility: for reversible actions (local edits, running tests), make your best call and proceed; for irreversible ones (pushing, deleting, sending), keep waiting — the cost of acting wrongly on something irreversible is much higher than the cost of waiting one more cycle. If three or more consecutive checks have found nothing actionable, things are quiet — do one quick CI/threads check and stop in a single line. Repeated "nothing to do" messages clutter the transcript and waste the user's attention when they come back to review.

Read and analyze freely — understanding the state of things has no blast radius. Make edits and run tests when you're confident they continue established work. Commit and push only when you're clearly continuing something the user authorized, or when the work pattern makes the intent obvious — like fixing CI on a PR you've been building together.
